methodological_rigor.justification: This single-center observational diagnostic-performance study includes 286 patients and 316 thyroid nodules, uses defined CNB categories, records complications, and recalculates performance in the surgically confirmed subset to address verification bias. Important limitations remain: there is no direct FNA comparator despite claims about first-line use, only 80 nodules had surgical confirmation, many malignant or benign classifications relied on CNB plus clinical/imaging correlation, CEUS, or one-year stability, and 39 lesions lacked definitive diagnosis. Statistics are appropriate for descriptive diagnostic accuracy and univariate risk-factor analysis, but confidence intervals are incompletely emphasized, no power calculation is reported, and multivariable modeling was not feasible because inconclusive events were limited.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The study is a real-world case series/low-quality cohort of selected thyroid nodules undergoing first-line CNB, so the Oxford level of evidence is 4. The clinical question is directly relevant because reducing nondiagnostic or indeterminate biopsy results could affect thyroid nodule management and unnecessary surgery. The manuscript reports patient-relevant diagnostic metrics, an unnecessary surgery rate of 6.3%, and no observed CNB complications, but lack of a prospective comparator prevents practice-changing conclusions.

reporting_quality.justification: STARD is the closest applicable standard because the manuscript evaluates diagnostic accuracy of CNB against surgical and composite reference standards. Core elements such as patient selection dates, biopsy technique, diagnostic categories, reference standards, performance metrics, subgroup analysis, and complications are reported, but the reference standard is heterogeneous and not applied to all nodules. Data and code are not deposited in a public repository; reproducibility rests on methods detail and summarized tables rather than open case-level data.

novelty_literature.justification: The work is a meaningful extension of prior CNB thyroid nodule studies by evaluating first-line CNB in a selected real-world cohort and separately presenting surgically confirmed performance. The manuscript itself cites earlier studies, meta-analyses, and guidelines supporting CNB for thyroid nodules, so the concept is not new. Its originality is mainly empirical and contextual, especially the emphasis on selected suspicious or large nodules and CEUS-assisted benign confirmation.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is generally readable and organized into standard diagnostic-study sections, with a quantitatively grounded abstract and useful flow and diagnostic-performance figures. It clearly acknowledges major biases in the discussion, including selection bias, composite benign standards, undiagnosed indeterminate lesions, and per-protocol analysis. Presentation problems include an incomplete-looking diagnostic-standard subsection, several awkward phrases and typographic errors, and some repeated claims about CNB's advantages over FNA despite the absence of an FNA comparator.

key_strengths: Clinically relevant real-world evaluation of first-line CNB for selected thyroid nodules.
Large lesion count for a single-center biopsy study with detailed CNB technique and diagnostic categories.
Reports both overall diagnostic performance and a surgically confirmed sensitivity analysis.
No hemorrhage, edema, infection, or needle tract seeding was observed.
key_concerns: No direct FNA comparison, so superiority or first-line replacement claims are not supported.
Composite reference standards and per-protocol exclusion of undiagnosed lesions may overestimate diagnostic performance.
Only 80 nodules were surgically confirmed, with very few benign surgical cases limiting specificity precision.
Single-center selected cohort limits generalizability to routine thyroid nodule screening.
chief_reviewer.rationale: This is a useful diagnostic case series with practical clinical relevance, but verification bias, lack of a comparator arm, and incomplete confirmation of indeterminate lesions keep it in a mid-tier range and require major revisions.
